notes.subject: the base commit
notes.note: R-f makes 2f8712a the tie-breaker, so every record in this artifact is a MEASUREMENT taken by driving a `git worktree` at that commit with its own `npm ci`, never a guess. The tooling that drove it lives in the target worktree, because it does not exist at the base commit; the analysed tree, the tool's own commit and the launcher options are in the sibling provenance file.

notes.subject: capture status
notes.note: CAPTURED. All 383 scenarios carry measured records: 382 were driven and recorded, and the remaining 1 carries an `unreachableReason` instead, because no HTTP request can reach it. `summary.captured` is true and `summary.baselinesPending` is 0. This is the secure cookie pass.

notes.subject: provenance
notes.note: Not in this file. It lives in the sibling `corpus.secure.json.provenance.json`, which carries the analysed worktree and its git HEAD, the tool's HEAD, the runtime, the launcher options and NODE_CONFIG of every segment, the seeding and object-store summaries, the fixture profiles, the payload-table digest, the route-manifest digest, and the SHA-256 of this file. Read the two together: a corpus without its sidecar does not say which tree it measured.

notes.subject: the two segments, and why there are two
notes.note: A capture of all 383 scenarios in ONE pass cannot complete at 2f8712a, and the cause is in the application. Driving `POST /api/admin/user/{userId}` reaches `admin.updateUser`, which hands its `User.findById` error to `request.fail` [lib/controllers/admin.js:160]; `request.fail` passes the Error to `h.response` [lib/util/routeParser.js:510]; hapi throws `Error: Cannot wrap an error` [@hapi/hapi/lib/toolkit.js:191] as an uncaught async exception and the process exits. Every case driven after it would record a transport failure that means nothing. So this artifact is the merge of two coherent segments on the SAME port, the SAME overlay and the SAME tool commit: segment A drove 382 scenarios in one pass with that route excluded, and segment B drove that route alone against a fresh server and database. No post-crash transport failure is committed here, and the merge is by scenario id so no record was reordered or overwritten by the other segment.

notes.subject: where the crash case sits, and why it is last
notes.note: The application-terminating route is the LAST record in this file rather than at its build-order position, so a consumer driving the corpus in order cannot be contaminated by the termination. MEASURED: in that order a full `replay.js --self-check --pass both` drove all 383 scenarios in one pass, reported that scenario as a match, and reported the application alive throughout. Read-only cases still precede mutating ones.

notes.subject: the payload table
notes.note: The `payloads` block holds the exact table that was merged over capture.js's built-in one with `--payloads` at capture time, so this artifact is re-drivable without reconstructing it. It closes the 21 route keys the built-in table did not cover - 23 scenarios, which were previously driven with an empty payload and labelled `unknown-payload`. Nineteen of them now drive a real success path; two keep the deliberately absent invitation id and record the not-found edge; and the four upload routes record the validation-failure edge for the reason stated on each of them. Payload values use unreserved characters deliberately: capture.js form-encodes with URLSearchParams (space becomes +) and replay.js with encodeURIComponent (space becomes %20), so a value containing a space is sent as a different number of bytes by the two tools, and MEASURED, that made the four upload routes echo a different `bytes` on replay. The encoding difference itself is a defect in those two tools, not in this artifact.

notes.subject: declared expectations, and the four that did not hold
notes.note: Every driven scenario carries an `expectation` whose clauses were derived from its own measured record, in the vocabulary both tools implement, so no scenario asserts nothing. Where capture.js had authored a clause of its own it is merged rather than replaced, and its wording is kept. Four of its clauses did NOT hold at 2f8712a under the committed configuration: the three `error-edge.asset-from-url.*` cases, which answer 501 because `config/default.yaml:3` sets `features.assets: false` and the handler returns notImplemented before any fetch; and `quirk.oauth.existing-user-succeeds`, whose `cross.bodiesDiffer` clause cannot discriminate two 302s with empty bodies. Each is kept verbatim under `declaredExpectation` with the result it produced, each scenario's notes state the mechanism, and `declaredExpectationsUnmet` counts them. Nothing was quietly relaxed.

notes.subject: the cookie pass
notes.note: The launcher runs the application with `isSecure` set, so Yar writes `session=<value>; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/` and the private-field patch [app.js:204-240] appends `Expires=<one year>; SameSite=None; Secure`. MEASURED: 18 responses in this pass carry that suffix, which AAP 0.6.1 calls the only way a silent no-op in the patch can be detected. Every attribute of every Set-Cookie is preserved in full - name, HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, Path, Domain, Max-Age and the presence and horizon of Expires - and only the cookie VALUE is replaced, by its digest, at capture time. The two passes are separate artifacts because they are separate measurements: `replay.js --secure-corpus` compares this one exactly instead of inferring a differential.

notes.subject: residual volatility, measured rather than assumed
notes.note: Five field classes still differ between two runs of the identical tree, and they are enumerated in `residualVolatility` with the mechanism, what normalizes them today, and the artifact that would close each one. They are generated values - an upload temp path, generated short codes, a bcrypt salt, a generated username - plus one order-dependent OAuth Location. Nothing else differed: a `--self-check` replay of 383 scenarios matched 367 of 382 driven records exactly in each pass, and the 15 that did not are those classes.

notes.subject: the port these records embed
notes.note: Absolute Location headers embed the port, and replay.js does not normalize an origin, so this corpus is only comparable against the port it was captured on: 3010, which is what `test/parity/server-overlay.json` declares and therefore what the documented replay command uses. Both segments and both cookie passes ran on it. A replay on another port must be given a corpus captured there.

notes.subject: the one approved deviation
notes.note: Exactly one scenario carries `expectedDeviation`: quirk.reply-chain.never-settles.image-download. The image branch of the file download never settles at baseline - recorded here as a timeout, which is a result - and AAP 0.7 decides the collision with "every route serves" in favour of serving, so the target answers 200 with the stream. A replay must report that as an APPROVED CHANGE, not a failure. The four header-resolved chains carry no marker and must not become collateral damage of that decision. `error-edge.asset-from-url.transport-refused` is NOT a deviation: it answers 501 under the committed configuration, as its notes explain.

notes.subject: the fifth auth-scheme outcome
notes.note: auth.outcome.lookup-error carries an `unreachableReason` rather than a record, and `summary.scenariosWithoutExpectation` counts it as the one scenario that asserts nothing. The "Auth error" branch needs the user lookup itself to fail [app.js:243-281], which none of the requests this corpus can issue causes, and simulating it would capture a different branch as though it were this one. The other four outcomes are driven and asserted independently, and replay reports the auth-scheme check as PASS with five outcomes accounted for.
notes.howToClose: MEASURED, and cheaper than a fault injected below the model boundary: the branch is reachable over HTTP from a session whose `userId` is not a castable ObjectId. `Model.findById('not-an-objectid')` REJECTS with a Mongoose CastError - measured on this runtime, without a live connection - and the scheme awaits that call inside the `try` whose catch returns `Boom.unauthorized('Auth error')`, so the rejection lands in exactly this outcome on BOTH trees with no application change. What is missing is a driver that can establish such a session: the session cookie is Iron-sealed by Yar, so only the capture driver can produce one, which makes the scenario a change to test/parity/capture.js's identity set (and the seeder it draws on) rather than to this artifact. A hand-written record here would be worse than the gap: capture.js would drop it on the next capture, and replay.js would try to drive it, find no such identity, and report the scenario as undriven - turning an honest gap into a broken gate.

notes.subject: the build state of the trees these records were taken from
notes.note: Neither the baseline worktree nor the target worktree had its built assets present: `public/components` and `public/css/base.css` are gitignored build outputs, and the baseline cannot produce them at all, because the digest-verified component fetch this migration adds does not exist at 2f8712a and the SCSS build fails without the component tree. One route records that state - the inert asset directory, driven at /cache-prefix-1/css/base.css, which answers 404 here - and its scenario says so. Every other record in this artifact is independent of build state: the two static pages render from templates and answer 200, and /robots.txt is a tracked file.

notes.subject: redirects
notes.note: Not followed. A Location header is part of the surface under comparison, and following it would replace the measurement with its consequence. The two redirect mechanisms differ and both appear here: the parser builds ABSOLUTE locations from the configured url, while the 401 branch of the error extension emits a RELATIVE /login. The derived `locationEndsWith` clauses therefore assert the path tail, which is what stays true across ports.

notes.subject: reCAPTCHA outcomes 3 to 6
notes.note: Unreachable over HTTP, and deliberately not chased. Under NODE_ENV=test the verify helper short-circuits on the isTest flag before any HTTP happens, so the 200, non-200, transport-failure and malformed-JSON branches cannot be reached through a route however the fixture is configured. They are exercised by direct module-level invocation in the fixture harness instead. Adding a reCAPTCHA secret to the overlay would not help - the short-circuit is on the environment, not on the secret - so none is added.

notes.subject: the Google client configuration
notes.note: Both OAuth handlers short-circuit without a configured client, and the server overlay does not declare one. This tool injects a fake client as an explicit top NODE_CONFIG layer so the OAuth branches are reachable at all. The values are not credentials: the token and profile endpoints are intercepted at the module boundary, so nothing authenticates against anything.

notes.subject: the OAuth existing-user identity
notes.note: The http fixture's seeding contract asks that its `existing` identity be seeded as a user, and the seeder does not seed it. The alignment call the fixture offers runs only inside the server process, and its environment contract has no identity variable, so neither artifact can be aligned from here. Rather than edit a sibling artifact, the existing-user branch is reached as a two-step sequence in which the new-user branch creates the account first. The gap is real and is recorded here; closing it in the seeder would make the sequence unnecessary but would not change what it captures.

notes.subject: cookie values
notes.note: The one value normalized at capture time. Session cookie values are already in the enumerated volatile set, so recording a digest instead of the value loses nothing that could have been compared, while keeping live session tokens out of a committed artifact. Every attribute that IS compared - name, HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, Path, Domain, Max-Age, and the presence and day horizon of Expires - is preserved in full, because the Expires horizon is the only way a silent no-op in the private-field cookie patch can be detected.

notes.subject: the cache-prefix timestamp in rendered asset URLs
notes.note: The one volatile value embedded in comparable HTML, and the only thing that differed between two consecutive captures of the same tree once cookies, Date and raw elapsed times are set aside. Every rendered page carries asset URLs of the form /cache-prefix-<epoch-millis>/<assetType>/<path>, because the string helper that builds them inlines the clock at RENDER time - it is not read from configuration, so no overlay can pin it and no fixture can make it stable. Measured: 20 of 242 read-only responses differed on this and on nothing else. It is a timestamp, so it is inside the enumerated volatile set, but it sits inside an href that is otherwise compared exactly - so a replay that does not normalize this pattern will report a difference on every rendered page. Normalize the digits between "/cache-prefix-" and the following "/" and compare the rest of the URL exactly; the prefix itself is configured and IS worth comparing.
